title: Debugging
blurb: Reading errors, isolating faults, fixing fast — a continuous skill.

lessons.title: Read the error
lessons.explain: A stack trace tells you WHAT went wrong and WHERE — read it bottom-up: the last line is the error type and message; the lines above show the call path. Most bugs are solved just by reading carefully.
lessons.example:
Traceback ...
  File "app.py", line 12, in main
KeyError: 'user_id'
objectives: Read a stack trace from the bottom up to find the actual error
Explain how stack trace changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example

commonMistakes: Reading a traceback top-down and getting lost in the call chain before finding the actual error message at the bottom.

lessons.title: Reading tracebacks & stack traces
objectives: Read a Python traceback from the bottom up
Explain how stack trace changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect stack trace with traceback and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A stack trace shows the sequence of function calls that led to where an error occurred. Read a Python traceback from the BOTTOM up: the bottom line shows the actual error and where it was raised; the lines above show the call chain that led there.
examples:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "app.py", line 10, in <module>
    result = divide(5, 0)
  File "app.py", line 3, in divide
    return a / b
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
# read bottom-up: the actual error is on the last line
commonMistakes: Reading a traceback top-down and getting lost in the call chain before finding the actual error message at the bottom.
lessons.careerRelevance: Fluently reading tracebacks is one of the fastest, most universally useful debugging skills.

lessons.title: A systematic method: reproduce, hypothesize, test
objectives: Apply a repeatable method instead of guessing
Explain how reproduc changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect reproduc with hypothesis and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: First, reproduce the bug reliably -- without a reliable reproduction, you can't confirm whether any change actually fixed it. Then form a specific hypothesis about the cause, and test it directly (often by printing a value you 'assumed' was correct).
examples:
# 1. Reproduce: run the exact steps that trigger the bug, confirm it happens every time
# 2. Hypothesize: 'I think X is None when it shouldn't be'
# 3. Test: print(X) right before the failing line to check
# 4. Bisection: if unsure WHERE it broke, check a point halfway through the logic, narrow from there
commonMistakes: Trying a fix before reliably reproducing the bug -- you can't tell if the fix actually worked or the bug just didn't happen to trigger that time.
lessons.careerRelevance: This method scales from tiny scripts to huge, unfamiliar codebases -- it's genuinely how experienced engineers debug.

lessons.title: Using a debugger: breakpoints & stepping
objectives: Use breakpoints and step through code interactively
Explain how breakpoint changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect breakpoint with step and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A breakpoint is a marked line where execution pauses so you can inspect the program's actual state -- variables, call stack, everything -- rather than just guessing. Stepping over a line runs it (including any function it calls) as one step; stepping into a line pauses at the FIRST line inside a called function instead, letting you follow execution deeper.
examples:
# in most debuggers:
# set a breakpoint on the suspicious line
# run until it pauses there
# inspect variables directly
# 'step over' vs 'step into' to control how deep you follow the call
commonMistakes: Relying only on print statements for a genuinely complex bug when a real debugger would let you pause and inspect state far more efficiently.
lessons.careerRelevance: Debugger fluency is expected in any real engineering role beyond the smallest scripts.

lessons.title: Common bug patterns: off-by-one, undefined names & edge cases
objectives: Recognize the most frequent categories of real bugs
Explain how off-by-one changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect off-by-one with undefined and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An off-by-one error is a loop or index boundary that's one step too far or too short (range(n) vs range(n+1)). An 'undefined' or 'not defined' error means the code references a name that was never assigned in the reachable scope.
examples:
for i in range(len(items) + 1):
    # off-by-one: this goes one index too far
    print(items[i])                    # IndexError on the last iteration

# undefined name: using a variable before it's ever assigned in that scope
commonMistakes: Assuming a loop or index boundary is correct without explicitly checking it against a small example by hand.
lessons.careerRelevance: These three patterns account for a huge share of real-world bugs across every language.

lessons.title: Silent & intermittent bugs
objectives: Recognize bugs that don't announce themselves clearly
Explain how silent changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect silent with intermittent and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A silent bug produces a wrong result without raising any visible error -- much harder to notice than a crash. An intermittent (flaky) bug doesn't reproduce consistently, often hinting at timing, randomness, or shared/mutable state being the real cause rather than a simple logic error.
examples:
# silent bug example: a function that returns 0 instead of raising an error
# when given invalid input -- looks like it 'worked', but the result is wrong

# flaky bug example: a test that passes 9 times out of 10 --
# investigate shared state or timing assumptions, not just 'bad luck'
commonMistakes: Dismissing a rarely-reproducing bug as 'probably nothing' instead of investigating shared state or timing as the likely real cause.
lessons.careerRelevance: Recognizing these two categories early saves enormous debugging time later.

lessons.title: Debugging habits: rubber duck, minimal repro & logging
objectives: Apply proven habits that make debugging faster
Explain how rubber duck changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect rubber duck with minimal reproducible example and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Rubber-duck debugging means explaining your code and reasoning out loud (even to an inanimate object) -- this often surfaces the bug yourself, mid-explanation. A minimal reproducible example is the smallest possible code that still reliably triggers the bug, with everything irrelevant removed -- shrinking it often reveals the actual cause.
examples:
# minimal reproducible example: strip a 500-line failing script down to
# the ~10 lines that still reproduce the bug -- the process of removing
# 'irrelevant' code often reveals what's actually causing it
commonMistakes: Sharing (or debugging from) the entire original codebase instead of first shrinking to a minimal reproducible example -- this buries the actual cause in noise.
lessons.careerRelevance: These habits are what separate efficient debugging from hours of unfocused searching.

lessons.title: Debugging in production vs locally
objectives: Reason about why a bug might only appear in one environment
Explain how production changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect production with used to work and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A bug that appears only 'in production' but not locally is usually caused by differences in environment: real data, configuration, dependency versions, or scale that don't match the local setup. Checking what recently changed (via git diff/log) is a strong first move when something 'used to work' but suddenly doesn't.
examples:
# common production-only causes:
# - real user data has an edge case your test data never included
# - a dependency version differs between local and production
# - production runs at a scale (data size, concurrency) local testing never reaches
commonMistakes: Assuming a production-only bug is a fluke or a hardware issue before checking for genuine environment/data/scale differences.
lessons.careerRelevance: This reasoning is essential for any real deployed system, not just local scripts.

lessons.title: Verifying fixes actually work
objectives: Confirm a fix addresses the real root cause, not just a symptom
Explain how verify changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect verify with expected output and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Always verify a fix resolves the ORIGINAL reported symptom, not just that some error disappeared -- a change can silence one symptom while leaving the real underlying bug (or a new one) unaddressed. Explicitly comparing 'expected output' vs 'actual output' turns a vague 'something's wrong' into a precise, checkable difference.
examples:
# before declaring a fix complete:
# 1. does it produce the ORIGINAL expected output, not just 'no error'?
# 2. does it still work for the edge cases identified earlier?
# 3. did anything else break as a side effect?
commonMistakes: Declaring a bug fixed as soon as the error message disappears, without confirming the actual expected behavior is now correct.
lessons.careerRelevance: This final verification step is what actually closes out a bug, rather than just relocating it.

options: a syntax error location
a marked line where execution pauses so you can inspect the program's state
the last line of a program

options: it isn't, actual output is always obviously wrong

interviewPreparation.q: Walk me through how you'd approach debugging an issue you've never seen before, live, in an interview.
interviewPreparation.a: Read the error/symptom carefully first rather than jumping to a fix, form a specific hypothesis about the cause, test that hypothesis directly (not just stare at the code), and narrow down systematically -- reproduce, hypothesize, test, repeat. Narrating this process out loud is itself part of what's being evaluated, not just arriving at the right answer.

interviewPreparation.q: How do you approach a bug that only happens intermittently, not every time?
interviewPreparation.a: Look for what's different between the runs that fail and the ones that succeed -- shared state between test runs, timing/race conditions, or an environment difference are common causes. Trying to reproduce it in isolation, and changing one variable at a time, is more productive than re-running the same thing hoping to catch it by luck.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the value of a minimal reproducible example when debugging?
interviewPreparation.a: Shrinking a large failing case down to the smallest version that still fails removes noise and irrelevant variables, making the actual cause much easier to spot -- and if you need to ask someone else for help, a minimal repro respects their time and gets you a faster, more useful answer than a 500-line dump.

interviewPreparation.q: Why is verifying a fix actually works more than just 'the error went away'?
interviewPreparation.a: The error going away could mean the actual bug is fixed, or it could mean the failure condition just isn't being hit anymore for an unrelated reason -- confirming the fix means re-running the exact scenario that originally failed and checking the expected output specifically, not just that nothing currently looks broken.

interviewPreparation.q: What would a good postmortem for a production bug include, beyond 'here's the fix'?
interviewPreparation.a: The actual root cause (not just the symptom), why it wasn't caught earlier (a missing test, an untested edge case, insufficient logging), and a concrete follow-up action that would catch this class of bug faster next time -- the goal is preventing a repeat, not just resolving this one instance.

careerApplications: Evaluated implicitly in every technical interview and every day on the job.

capstone.title: Diagnose and document one genuinely hard bug, from symptom to root cause
capstone.description: Unlike the existing 'Debug a broken repo' project (many small bugs, breadth-focused), this capstone is about depth: take one bug that resists a quick fix -- something intermittent, silent, or only reproducible under specific conditions -- and work it methodically from first symptom to verified root cause, using the full systematic method (reproduce, hypothesize, test) rather than guessing. Document the investigation as you'd write it up for a teammate, not just the final fix.
deliverables: A bug that genuinely isn't obvious on first read -- intermittent, silent, or only reproducible under specific conditions, not a one-line typo
A written investigation log showing the actual hypotheses you tested and what each one ruled out, not just the final correct answer presented as if it were obvious from the start
Use of either a real debugger (breakpoints/stepping) or a bisection approach to narrow down the cause, not just print-statement guessing
A verified fix -- proof the specific failure no longer reproduces, not just 'it seems fixed'
A short postmortem-style write-up: root cause, why it wasn't caught earlier, and one concrete change (a test, a log line, an assertion) that would catch this class of bug faster next time
capstone.portfolioTips: The investigation log -- including the hypotheses that turned out to be WRONG -- is more valuable to show than a clean final answer. It's direct evidence of a real, methodical process, which is exactly what a live debugging interview is trying to assess.

industryUsage.usage: Widely known for blameless postmortem culture after production incidents -- documenting root cause and what would catch a similar bug faster next time, rather than just noting who fixed it.
Uses a formal 'Correction of Error' process after significant incidents, requiring genuine root-cause analysis rather than treating a quick fix as the end of the investigation.
Live debugging exercises (reading a stack trace, forming hypotheses, narrowing down a cause under time pressure) are a common, explicitly practiced format in its engineering interviews.
